data.title: Telecom Fraud in 2025: Emerging Threats and Smarter Defenses
data.summary: Telecom fraud has become increasingly sophisticated—and costly. In 2023 alone, fraud in the global telecom industry surged by 12%, amounting to an estimated $38.95 billion in losses. As fraud tactics grow more advanced, staying ahead requires smarter, faster, and more adaptive defenses. Here are the top trends reshaping the telecom fraud landscape—and how the industry can rise to the challenge. 1. AI-Powered Scams Generative AI tools like FraudGPT enable fraudsters to deploy hyper-personalized phishing campaigns, create malware automatically, and generate deepfake content at scale. These AI-driven scams double the speed and realism of attacks, making traditional firewall systems unable to detect these types of frauds. 2. SIM Box Fraud SIM Box devices reroute international calls through local networks, bypassing interconnect charges. This “bypass fraud” has costed carriers roughly $3.1 billion annually as of 2023. These devices exploit VoIP links, making global calls appear local. 3. International Revenue Share Fraud (IRSF) In IRSF, fraudsters direct unsuspecting callers to premium-rate numbers, profiting from artificially generated traffic. It remains among the industry’s most lucrative fraud schemes. 4. AI-Powered Deepfake Voice Vishing Voice cloning lets fraudsters impersonate executives or officials in real-time. These deepfake voice calls have enabled highly convincing “vishing” scams which has caused direct financial losses, prompting urgent investment in voice biometrics and authentication systems. 5. AI-Enhanced Phishing Using generative AI, fraudsters now craft ultra-polished voice calls or WhatsApp messages that mimic credible communications from banks or telcos. AI Bots automate voice scams that bypass legacy firewall solutions and deliver near-human interactions, leading to higher success rates. 6. Wangiri Fraud: AI-Powered Callback Scams Modern Wangiri scams involve AI-driven auto-dialers that place thousands of brief calls, enticing the receiver into returning premium-rate calls. This results in billions in revenue losses for telecom operators. Turning the Tide with AI-Driven Defense These evolving threats underscore a critical reality – AI is a double-edged sword. data.title: The Critical Role of DLT in Combating SMS Fraud
data.summary: SMS remains a vital channel for Application-to-Person (A2P) communication, supporting critical functions like OTPs, banking alerts, and promotional messaging. However, the integrity of A2P messaging is increasingly compromised by fraudulent activities. In 2023 alone, between 19.8 billion and 35.7 billion fraudulent messages were sent, accounting for 4.8% of global messaging traffic, leading to significant financial losses for businesses and operators. What is Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT)? Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT), commonly associated with blockchain, is a decentralized database where data is recorded across multiple nodes. Each transaction is time-stamped, immutable, and cryptographically secured, ensuring data integrity and transparency. This decentralized nature makes DLT ideal for maintaining verifiable records, especially in sectors prone to data manipulation. Why DLT in Telecom? In the telecom sector, DLT offers a robust solution to verify sender identities, register and validate message templates, and provide traceability for every message. By creating a trusted ecosystem, DLT minimizes the chances of malicious activities, ensuring that only pre-approved entities and content can interact with end-users. How DLT Secures SMS Networks Sender Registration: Enterprises must register on the DLT platform, ensuring only verified entities can send messages. Template Approval: Each message template undergoes an approval process, eliminating spam or misleading messages. Consent Management: Customers’ consent for receiving messages is recorded and auditable, giving control to the recipients. Real-Time Tracking: Every message can be traced back to its origin, with an immutable audit trail deterring spoofing and unauthorized routes. Limitations of DLT While DLT enhances security, it isn’t a comprehensive solution. It doesn’t address phishing via malicious links, AI-generated scam messages, or cross-border frauds. Moreover, its effectiveness depends on full ecosystem compliance; without universal adoption, its benefits can be limited. The Future of DLT in Telecom Security For DLT to reach its full potential, integration with advanced threat intelligence systems and AI-powered anomaly detection is essential. Global collaboration among operators, regulators, and enterprises can extend DLT’s scope beyond SMS to other communication platforms, ensuring secure and trusted digital communication.

data.title: Strengthening SMS Networks Against Modern Threats
data.summary: Telecom networks today face an escalating threat from a growing underground model known as Fraud-as-a-Service (FaaS). It allows fraudsters to offer ready-made fraud kits, enabling scammers to exploit SMS networks for malicious purposes. The financial toll of these scams is staggering, with telecom operators, enterprises, and end-users all suffering the consequences. The Rise of FaaS in SMS Fraud Fraud-as-a-Service is fueling a global surge in SMS scams, hitting telecom operators with major financial and reputational damage. FaaS and Its Impact on the SMS Network FaaS works by enabling fraudsters to manipulate SMS traffic through various illicit methods, including: Grey Routes & SMS Bypass Fraud: Fraudsters use unlicensed routes to bypass legitimate networks, leading to lost revenue for telecom operators and degraded service for customers. SIM Farms: Criminals use large-scale SIM card farms to send out fraudulent messages in bulk, which are often used for scams or spam. SMS Phishing (Smishing): Scammers use fraudulent SMS messages to trick users into sharing sensitive information, leading to identity theft or financial losses. SMS Pumping Fraud: This technique involves tricking users into unknowingly sending premium-rate messages, adding charges to their phone bills. Flash Calls vs. SMS OTP Fraud: Fraudsters use flash calls (calls that disconnect immediately) to verify accounts, bypassing SMS OTP (One-Time Password) authentication systems, leading to unauthorized access to accounts. How Telecom Companies Are Fighting Back To combat this growing threat, telecom companies are adopting advanced technologies and strategies: AI-driven fraud detection: By analyzing SMS patterns in real-time, telecom companies can identify and block suspicious activity before it causes harm. Next-gen firewalls & traffic filtering: Telecom companies can use firewalls and traffic filters to block grey routes and prevent unauthorized access to their networks. Regulatory compliance & stricter authentication: Telecom operators must adhere to regulatory guidelines and implement stronger authentication methods to ensure secure SMS exchanges. Cross-industry collaboration: Telecom companies must work together with other industry players against FaaS networks, sharing intelligence and tools to combat telecom frauds. Fraud-as-a-Service is a growing threat to telecom networks, operators, and consumers. According to the Mobile Ecosystem Forum (MEF), 39% of consumers across ten surveyed countries encountered at least one SMS scam attempt in the past year. By understanding the mechanics of SMS scams and adopting next-gen AI-powered fraud management like Armour, telecom companies can protect their revenue, reputation, and customer trust.

Unlike traditional rule-based systems, AI-driven fraud detection evolves continuously, identifying anomalies and stopping fraudulent activities before they cause damage. AI-Powered Fraud Detection Techniques AI employs multiple techniques to combat fraud effectively: Behavioral Analysis: By monitoring user behavior, AI identifies deviations that may indicate fraudulent activity, such as unusual transaction patterns or login attempts. Anomaly Detection: AI detects irregularities in real-time, flagging suspicious activities that deviate from normal usage trends. Predictive Analytics: Using historical data, AI forecasts potential fraud attempts and enables proactive security measures. Real-Time Threat Monitoring: AI-driven systems provide continuous monitoring, allowing instant responses to fraudulent activities and minimizing financial losses. The Evolving Fraud Landscape Fraudsters are adapting, employing AI themselves to bypass security measures. From deepfake scams to AI-generated phishing attacks, threats are becoming more sophisticated. However, AI also evolves in response, strengthening security through continuous learning and adaptation. GenAI is particularly impactful, as it helps security systems simulate potential fraud attempts and prepare countermeasures in advance. Data Privacy: AI relies on vast datasets, raising concerns about user privacy and compliance with regulations like GDPR. AI Bias: Improperly trained AI models may exhibit biases, potentially leading to unfair fraud assessments. What’s Next? data.title: Geordie Shore star and illegal finfluencer sentenced for promoting high-risk investments on social media
data.summary:
Aaron Chalmers, a reality TV star and social media content creator, and finfluencer Jason Agbodza have been sentenced for illegally promoting an unauthorised foreign exchange trading scheme on social media.

Chalmers, 39 and from Newcastle, was sentenced at City of London Magistrates Court. He previously pleaded guilty and today (19 November) was fined £3,072 and ordered to pay costs of £2,836.Having risen to fame on Geordie Shore, Chalmers has more than 2 million followers on Instagram. Agbodza, 35, of London, was also fined £1,173 and ordered to pay costs of £2,114 after pleading guilty.Both men encouraged followers to invest in foreign exchange (forex or FX) trading through contracts for difference (CFDs), without being authorised to promote them. CFDs are high-risk derivatives, and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has previously found that approximately 80% of customers lose money when investing in them.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market integrity at the FCA, said:'With more than two million Instagram followers, Chalmers exploited his online influence to illegally promote investments to a vast audience. Agbodza made significant profits from an unlawful investment scheme. These cases send a clear message: we will take decisive action against those that break the law and put consumers at risk.'Separately, earlier this year the FCA issued cautions to 2 individuals for posting illegal financial promotions on social media. The cautions will appear on their criminal records.The FCA is also calling on social media platforms to do more to stop illegal financial promotions at source. Google, Bing (Microsoft), Meta, X and TikTok have agreed to restrict paid-for financial services advertising to FCA-authorised firms, helping to reduce scam adverts significantly. But illegal promotions remain prevalent. During the FCA's international week of action on unlawful finfluencers, 66% of illegal financial adverts identified on social media were linked to firms or individuals already on the FCA Warning List. Platforms need to monitor more closely and intervene faster.Notes to editorsAaron Chalmers' date of birth is 26/05/1987. data.title: The courage to change
data.summary:
Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at TheCityUK National Conference 2026.

Our willingness to do things differently in this country has helped make our financial services sector one of the most innovative in the world.We didn’t get here by accident.It took ambitious firms, given the right amount of room to experiment.The FCA recognised the importance of pushing the boundaries with Project Innovate in 2014.And the world’s first Regulatory Sandbox in 2016, allowing firms to test innovative ideas with dedicated FCA support.By 2024, fintech was the most significant job source in UK financial services.Fintech firms contribute positively to growth, productivity and infrastructure.No wonder the UK is Europe’s top spot for fintech investment.But we can’t take that position for granted.Investment is down. Global competition is up. Funding is getting harder to come by.And operational disruption is no longer a matter of if, but when.We’ve recently seen the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange robbed of more than $6 billion.And a global tech outage that left millions of employees without the tools they need to do their jobs.Market integrity risks have never been greater.That's not a reason to hold back on innovation.If anything, it’s a reason to keep going. We can’t solve these challenges if we stand still.But we need to be clear-eyed along the way.That doesn’t mean certain.None of us can wait for perfect information.You decide whether to build, hire or invest before knowing if the idea will work.We often need to decide whether to act – and how – without the full picture.Uncertainty comes with the territory.And in a rapidly changing world, we need to be comfortable making decisions in the face of it.The decisions that got us here were made that way. The ones ahead will be too.

data.title: Insurance firms called on to improve claims handling

data.title: FCA launches world-first platform giving firms new insight into AI innovation

data.title: UK financial watchdogs clarify cyber expectations as attacks rise
data.summary:
UK’s financial regulators are proposing new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow.

The Bank of England’s most recent Systemic Risk Survey cited cyber as one of the risks that would have the greatest impact on the UK financial system. October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the FCA in 5 years, and the highest in the past 18 months, 52% above the previous high recorded in May 2025.In response, the Bank, FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) are bringing together existing requirements and lessons from supervisory experience to give firms greater clarity about what is expected of them.The proposed guidance aligns with recognised cyber frameworks, including the National Cyber Security Centre’s (NCSC) Cyber Assessment Framework. It sets out how firms should manage their cyber risk and resilience without imposing rigid rules, giving firms flexibility in how they meet the expectations in a fast-evolving threat environment.It covers key areas, including how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from cyber risks and incidents. Firms need strong cyber controls to help keep them safe, support well-functioning markets and protect consumers.Nikhil Rathi, Chief Executive of the FCA, said: ‘Technology moves fast, and so do cyber threats. The financial sector has a crucial role in tackling those threats, including through products like cyber insurance.‘Our response shouldn’t always be more rules. Firms have asked us for clarity about what good cyber resilience looks like. This guidance provides it, helping strengthen their resilience, protect clients and the services they rely on.’Katharine Braddick, CEO of the PRA and Deputy Governor at the Bank of England, said:‘Cyber attacks are becoming more frequent, complex and dangerous. Regulators need confidence both that firms have strong cyber controls and that they can detect, contain and recover quickly from incidents. Today’s proposed guidance builds on latest understanding to help firms do that.’Dr Richard Horne, NCSC Chief Executive Officer, said:‘We know cyber threats are becoming increasingly frequent and sophisticated, making it more important than ever that organisations can withstand and recover from cyber incidents.‘The National Cyber Security Centre welcomes this proposed guidance, which will help firms better understand, assess, and strengthen their cyber resilience, in line with our Cyber Assessment Framework.’Helping firms prepare for AI and quantum risksSeparately, the regulators are publishing additional ‘effective practices’, building on the cyber guidance to help firms practically prepare for specific cyber risks linked to rapid developments in AI and the potential emergence of quantum computing. The effective practices include firms tackling vulnerabilities to threat actors using AI, and encourage firms to consider the implications of quantum computing, which could undermine the public-key cryptography that underpins financial transactions. These materials reflect the regulators’ position and expertise that allows them to act on the newest risks in the sector, guiding firms through an uncertain and rapidly developing area.Notes to editorsThe FCA, PRA and the Bank have jointly published a consultation on cyber risk and resilience management.The consultation closes on 26 February 2027.Firms, trade associations, technology providers and other interested stakeholders are encouraged to respond. Feedback will inform the final guidance next year.The proposed guidance is appliable to firms in scope of the regulators' existing operational resilience requirements. The approach regulators have taken also reflects the FCA’s focus on smarter, proportionate regulation, providing greater clarity through guidance where new rules are not necessary. This gives firms flexibility in how they meet existing regulatory expectations as cyber risks continue to evolve.The proposed guidance key foundational cyber risk and resilience areas include:Embedding cyber risk and resilience in governance and risk management, with clear roles and accountabilities, appropriate board and senior management oversight, defined risk appetite, and regular reporting and assurance.Identifying and understanding critical IT infrastructure and cyber risk, maintaining up-to-date inventories and maps of critical assets, systems, data and dependencies, and assessing relevant threats, vulnerabilities and potential impacts.Protecting critical IT infrastructure from cyber threats, applying proportionate controls including secure configuration, vulnerability and patch management, identity and access management, data protection, and controls over third parties and supply chains.Detecting cyber events and incidents promptly, through effective monitoring and detection capabilities, defined alerting and escalation processes, and regular testing of firms' ability to identify potential attacks.Responding to and recovering from cyber incidents effectively, with tested response and recovery plans, clear decision-making and communications arrangements, capabilities to contain attacks and restore services, and processes to identify and address lessons learned.The additional material on AI and quantum computing is not open for formal consultation. However, the regulators are keen to understand from industry whether this type of support is useful and what they would like to see in future.A recent Bank of England and FCA survey found 88% of respondents expect frontier AI cyber capabilities to have a moderate or high impact on their risk profile over the next 2 years.In the same survey, 64% said vulnerability management and patching had seen the greatest increase in management attention due to awareness of frontier AI.

data.title: What we’re learning from firms engaging with our innovation services
data.summary: Three themes stand out: the growing use of AI, innovation crossing traditional sector boundaries, and financial inclusion.As firms develop new products, services and business models, many engage with us through our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways to understand how regulation applies to their proposition or to test innovative ideas in a controlled environment.Looking across applications lets us observe emerging trends. It helps us understand how technologies are evolving, and identify emerging regulatory questions.In turn, this supports our wider work and helps us keep pace with developments across financial services.Applications at a glance37% involved AI (up from 31% in 2025), making it the most common technology theme.92% of the firms engaging with our services were doing so for the first time, highlighting continued demand from new innovators.64% of proposed solutions included a retail element, showing continued focus on consumer-facing innovation.The growing use of AIFirms are focusing increasingly on how to deploy, oversee and govern AI in their business models.They’re looking at how to use AI to help consumers better understand and manage their finances, support businesses with payment processes, and provide customers with more personalised guidance and support.Regulation and innovation are working in tandem to deploy new technologies safely and build consumer protection into new products from the outset.Innovation is becoming more interconnectedInnovation does not always fit neatly into traditional sector categories. While payments and digital assets represented the largest sector-specific portion of recent applications, cross-sector propositions have also been common, representing around one-third of applications.Many firms are combining technologies, data, payments and consumer-facing services in new ways. As a result, innovative technologies are increasingly crossing traditional sector boundaries and requiring firms to consider how existing governance, accountability, data use and regulatory frameworks apply.A recent example is our stablecoins cohort in the Regulatory Sandbox. Stablecoin business models often cut across traditional sector boundaries, combining elements of payments, digital assets, and financial market activity. The cohort brought together firms intending to issue UK stablecoins to test how proposed requirements could operate in practice and provide evidence to support policy development.Financial inclusionFirms continue to focus on how to improve consumer access to and engagement with financial services. They’re not only exploring new technologies, but also considering how these tools can help address practical consumer challenges.Applications this year have included propositions aimed at improving consumer understanding, accessibility, personalised support, and access to financial services for underserved groups.A large proportion of proposed solutions included a retail element, indicating that most firms remain focused on end consumers.What we’re learning about Sandbox participation over timeWe are looking beyond current application trends to understand the longer-term experience of firms that have participated in the Regulatory Sandbox.Our preliminary research suggests that, as of September 2026, around 71% of them are still active. We are continuing this analysis to better understand the ongoing commercial success of participating firms and whether their original propositions have continued to operate.We have also been looking to understand at which point of their growth firms engage with the Regulatory Sandbox.We’ve found that the service is particularly relevant at an early stage of a firm’s development, with around 70% of applications coming from firms that are 0 to 2 years old.Demand is strongest when firms are still developing their business models, products and approaches to compliance, and seeking to understand how regulation applies as they refine and validate innovative propositions.Looking aheadApplications to our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways give us an early view of the technologies, business models and the regulatory questions that firms are exploring.They also provide insight into developments beyond the UK.We’re continuing to engage with international firms seeking to enter the UK market and sharing insights with overseas regulators and innovation initiatives. This helps us to understand global innovation trends.The trends we have seen so far suggest that innovation is scaling up, becoming more sophisticated, and more focused on addressing real-world consumer needs.We’ll continue to engage with firms as technology develops. One way we’re doing this is through thematic cohorts, which explore key areas in greater depth.Following our Regulatory Sandbox stablecoins cohort, applications to a new climate scenarios cohort opened on 1 October 2026. The cohort invites firms and specialists to test innovative approaches to climate scenario analysis and risk assessment, supporting wider work on sustainable finance and climate-related risks.Firms developing new ideas should consider how existing regulation applies to their proposition, how they can test and scale innovation successfully, and what safeguards will deliver good outcomes for consumers and markets.Our innovation services help firms answer these questions. They also let us test policy approaches and gather evidence on how regulation works in practice. This helps inform smarter, more proportionate regulation.We’re here to support innovators across financial services, helping ensure the UK remains one of the best places in the world to develop, test and scale innovative propositions.

data.title: FCA proposes greater pension investment flexibility to support long-term value for savers
data.summary:
Workplace pension providers could have greater flexibility to invest for the long term under proposals from the FCA, helping them deliver better outcomes for savers while ensuring savers' interests remain protected.

The FCA is consulting on excluding certain performance-linked fees from the charge cap for default funds in workplace pensions it regulates.Performance-linked fees are common in private markets, including private equity, venture capital and private credit. The proposed change would give providers greater flexibility to access a broader range of investments where this could help improve long-term returns and value for savers.The FCA is clear that greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Providers should carefully weigh potential returns, risks and costs when making investment decisions, and any higher charges should be justified by the additional value delivered to savers.Alongside the proposed flexibility, the FCA is proposing safeguards covering transparency, fair allocation of fees between savers and scrutiny of how private assets are valued. Providers and Independent Governance Committees would need access to the information necessary to assess whether performance-linked fees offer value for money.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market integrity at the FCA, said: 'People's pension savings should work hard for them. We want providers to have greater choice over how they invest for the long term where this can deliver better outcomes for savers.'But greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Any higher charges must be justified by additional value, with firms carefully weighing returns, risks and costs when deciding what is in savers' best interests.'The proposals would bring FCA rules more closely into line with the regime for trust-based pension schemes, where certain performance-linked fees have been excluded from the charge cap since 2023.Greater alignment would support competition and choice and reduce unnecessary complexity for providers operating across both parts of the market.The proposals would give providers an option, not an obligation, to use the exemption. Providers should do so only where it is in savers' interests, and they can meet the relevant protections.The FCA is seeking responses by 14 January 2027 and currently expects to make final rules in summer 2027 following consideration of feedback.Notes to editorsThe consultation is open until Thursday 14 January 2027. Read CP26/40: Exempting performance fees from the workplace pensions charge cap.This work is a priority under the FCA's Pensions Regulatory Priorities (PDF) and forms part of the wider pensions reform.In 2023, the Government changed the rules so certain performance fees sit outside the limit on charges, with protections for members. The proposals build on changes made for trust-based schemes in 2023, while reflecting developments in private markets and strengthening protections in areas such as how investments are valued.The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA .

data.title: Man sentenced over £154m fake takeover bid targeting UK-listed company
data.summary:
Christopher Woolcott has today been given a 2-year prison sentence, suspended for 2 years, after staging a £154m fake takeover bid for Touchstone Exploration Inc.

He was also ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work and to pay costs of £4,627.73.Mr Woolcott built a sizeable stake in Touchstone, an oil and gas listed company. He then launched a bogus bid to drive up its share price. To give the bid credibility, Mr Woolcott invented several identities, forged takeover documents using Chat GPT and met Touchstone’s chief executive at a central London hotel under a false name. Touchstone ultimately determined that the bid was not legitimate.Had his plan succeeded, he stood to gain as much as £70,000 through the sale of his shares.The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) used a combination of its transaction reporting data, phone records, receipts, CCTV footage and evidence seized to identify Mr Woolcott as the person behind the fraud.Investigators traced three phone numbers used by different supposed individuals to contact Touchstone, to the same handset, and combined voter-register, open source research and FCA trading data to narrow down potential suspects. A parking payment also placed Mr Woolcott’s car near a Ryman store where the forged documents were sent from.Searches of Mr Woolcott's home and workplace later recovered the mobile phone linked to the fabricated identities, including a purported private equity partner, his supposed colleague and a fictitious solicitor.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:'Mr Woolcott's fake takeover bid was a calculated attempt to profit by manipulating the market.'Our investigators followed an extensive evidence trail, exposed the fraud and identified the person behind the ruse.‘Anyone tempted to manipulate our markets should know that we are fully committed to identifying, investigating and taking action against those who seek to break the law.'In sentencing, Judge Karu said Mr Woolcott’s operation was deliberate, sophisticated, and planned in which four false identities and forged documents were used to hoodwink Touchstone Exploration Inc with a false takeover bid.Mr Woolcott pleaded guilty on 10 September 2026 to 1 count of fraud by false representation and 3 counts of making a false instrument.The investigation demonstrates how the FCA uses its full range of enforcement powers to disrupt financial crime and protect market integrity.The FCA opened its criminal investigation in March 2025, formally charged Mr Woolcott 16 months later and secured guilty pleas within 18 months of launching the case.Notes to editorsChristopher Woolcott, of Greenwich, London, was born on 23 April 1982.On 10 September 2026, Woolcott pleaded guilty at Westminster Magistrates’ Court to:1 count of fraud by false representation, contrary to sections 1 and 2 of the Fraud Act 2006; and3 counts of making a false instrument, contrary to sections 1 and 6 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981. Fraud by false representation is punishable by a fine and/or up to 10 years’ imprisonment.Making a false instrument is punishable on indictment by a fine and/or up to 10 years’ imprisonment.On 10 November 2026 at Southwark Crown Court, Mr Woolcott was sentenced to:a 2 year sentence, suspended for 2 years, and ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work and pay costs of £4627.73; anda 14 months custodial sentence for each of the three forgery offences, to run concurrently with the two year suspended sentence.The FCA opened its criminal investigation in March 2025.Touchstone Exploration Inc is listed on AIM and the Toronto Stock Exchange. It was not under investigation by the FCA in connection with this case.Read the previous FCA press release: Man pleads guilty to fraud and forgery offences relating to fake takeover approach.Tackling market abuse and financial crime is a priority under the FCA’s 5-year strategy.

data.title: The not-so-fine print: making consumer contracts fair
data.summary: How many of us read the terms and conditions of a contract before buying a financial product?Contracts hold the detail that shapes everyone's financial life, whether you're taking out a loan, insuring your holiday, or signing up for a crypto wallet.All firms are responsible for making sure that terms in their consumer contracts comply with the fairness and transparency requirements of the Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015. When those terms don’t comply, our Consumer Contracts team has powers to challenge firms directly.This work shows how we use the full range of powers Parliament has given us, not only those in financial services legislation, to tackle harm.Here's why it matters: if a term is found to be unfair, it's not just unenforceable – consumers may be due redress too. That's why it pays for firms to get this right from the start.We review contract terms identified through our supervision of firms, information on social media, and referrals from consumers and other external stakeholders. When we take action We consider our rules and guidance, including the Consumer Duty, when deciding whether to act and which of our regulatory tools to use. Where we raise concerns about the fairness or transparency of terms, we expect firms to: Amend or delete the relevant terms so that the contract is fair and transparent, and stop relying on those terms in existing contracts.Pay redress to consumers if the firm’s use of the terms has caused harm; andIn some cases, give us a voluntary undertaking under the CRA. Where necessary, we can apply for a court injunction to prevent a firm from using or enforcing the term against its customers. We can also seek a court order requiring it to pay redress. Examples of cases we've tackledA crypto firm agreed to stop charging excessive storage fees which, in some cases, could exceed £40,000 a year. We intervened after finding it had charged inactive customers a disproportionate amount. The firm removed the term and paid redress to affected consumers.A financial adviser updated its contracts after trying to charge a customer £800 for time spent handling a complaint. The charge was included in its terms and conditions, but we considered the term unfair because it could put people off making legitimate complaints. We also considered it inconsistent with the Consumer Duty and our own rules.A travel insurer clarified unclear terms about what counted as a 12-hour delay and paid out £18,000 in redress to customers whose claims had been wrongly denied. Here, ambiguous wording was the problem, so we pushed for clearer terms that told consumers exactly what they were entitled to.A lender improved the terms of a new credit product to give clearer information on costs and cancellation rights after we raised concerns ahead of launch. This is a good example of intervening early, through the authorisations process, to prevent unfair terms making it to market in the first place.What we expect of firmsFirms should regularly check that their consumer contracts are fair, clear and transparent, and that they're being used fairly in practice. In practice, that means:Taking into account consumers’ legitimate interests when designing contracts.Using plain language, so customers understand what they're agreeing to: for example, what they might have to pay and what rights they have. Nobody should need a law degree to understand what they're signing up to. Avoiding surprises, by making important terms – fees, cancellation rights, variations, exclusions, complaints – easy to spot.Reviewing contracts regularly to stay compliant with the latest requirements, rulings and judgments, and to learn from complaints, claims, cancellations, fees, customer outcomes and other data.Testing whether customers actually understand key terms – not just assuming they do.Improving staff training to ensure staff meet the standards set out in product literature, including contracts. Using complaints data to identify potentially unfair or unclear contract terms and make appropriate changes.How to report concerns about unfair or unclear terms to usConcerned about an unfair or unclear term in a financial services firm’s consumer contract? You can report it to us using our form. We can't always tell you what action we've taken, but, we can assure you, every report we receive gets considered.

data.title: FCA acts to protect consumers facing demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments
data.summary:
We've intervened and Ethica Resolve Limited (Ethica), an FCA authorised firm that services and collects debt on behalf of creditors, has agreed to restrictions. These follow demands it made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes.

Ethica is acting on behalf of West 28th Street Limited (West 28), which bought disguised remuneration loans from a third party. West 28 is not authorised or regulated by the FCA.Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries. HMRC has published guidance for those affected.Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they're unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.Under the requirements we’ve agreed, Ethica:Will write to affected consumers, explaining that they do not have an enforceable obligation to make payment at this stage. (This means they do not need to pay now while regulatory and legal issues relating to the purported loans are resolved.)Will not make further demands for payment from affected consumers in the current proposed court claim while regulatory and legal issues are resolved.Additionally, Ethica and West 28 will not ask a court to make a judgment against someone who has not responded to a legal claim. This is known as a ‘default judgment’. However, consumers should not ignore any formal court documents they receive on this issue. They should consider seeking independent legal or debt advice before deciding what to do.Additional protections for vulnerable consumers are being put in place and Ethica will identify affected consumers who may be vulnerable.It has not yet been decided whether the debts can be enforced, which may be decided by a court. The requirements agreed protect consumers from avoidable harm while the relevant regulatory and legal issues are resolved. Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.

data.title: Looking back to move forward: why reviewing our rules matters
data.summary: Markets evolve. Consumer behaviour changes. Technology creates new opportunities and risks. Rules that were appropriate when they were introduced may need to be updated, simplified or, in some cases, removed altogether.That is why the FCA regularly reviews its rules.

data.title: FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime
data.summary:
A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.Notes to editorsRead more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

data.title: Act now to be resilient in the quantum future
data.summary: Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.What firms need to do nowSo, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to:Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.How we are supporting firmsWe are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.You can find more information:NCSC, Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptographyG7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sectorCMORG, Guidance for post-quantum cryptography

data.title: New FCA rules bring ESG rating providers into UK regulation for the first time
data.summary:
New UK rules for environmental, social and governance (ESG) rating providers will raise standards in the market, helping investors to make better informed decisions.

The new framework brings ESG rating providers into FCA regulation for the first time, covering a market that plays an important role in investment decisions. The rules are designed to improve the transparency, reliability and comparability of ESG ratings, helping build confidence in the information investors rely on. The regime applies to firms or organisations providing ESG ratings and assessments to ensure reliability across the market. The FCA has published guidance to help firms understand whether they may be in scope. Laura Dawes, director of authorisations and sustainable finance at the FCA, said: 'Trusted information is essential for well-functioning markets. These rules will help improve transparency and raise standards across the ESG ratings market while supporting competition, innovation and growth. 'Firms should check now whether they are in scope and start preparing for authorisation. We'll continue to provide practical support to help them prepare.'The new framework introduces requirements covering transparency, governance, systems and controls, the management of conflicts of interest, and engagement with users of ESG ratings and rated entities. It is designed to be proportionate to firms' size and activities and is informed by international and existing standards. Firms that may be in scope should start preparing now. ESG rating providers operating in the UK market will need to apply for FCA authorisation from 24 June 2027. The FCA will provide webinars and access to its Pre-Application Support Service to help firms prepare. Firms should now: understand whether the framework could apply to their activities review the final rules and guidanceconsider whether they need FCA authorisationstart preparing for implementationengage early with FCA support servicesNotes to editorsRead the FCA’s Policy Statement and final rules, PS26/22, ‘ESG ratings: final regime’.The new framework takes effect on 29 June 2028. From that date, firms providing ESG ratings in the UK will need FCA authorisation and to have the relevant permission before carrying on that activity, unless an exemption applies.ESG rating providers operating in the UK market will need to apply for FCA authorisation from 24 June 2027. We are staggering application periods and encourage firms to apply as early as possible within their window. ESG ratings generally assess how companies or other entities, assets, or financial products perform against environmental, social and governance criteria. They are used by asset managers, lenders, benchmark administrators and others to inform capital allocation decisions and manage risk, among other uses. The approach is shaped by international standards, including recommendations from the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO). The final rules follow the FCA’s consultation, CP25/34, which opened on 1 December 2025 and closed on 31 March 2026. The regulatory framework follows government legislation bringing the provision of ESG ratings within the FCA’s remit in October 2025. 95% of respondents to the government’s consultation supported the move. The regime regulates how ESG ratings are produced, governed and communicated. It does not prescribe a particular sustainability view or methodology. There is strong investor demand for ESG information. The FCA's Financial Lives Survey 2024 found 72% of adults with investments or a defined contribution pension wanted their investments to do some good as well as provide a financial return.

data.title: FCA sets expectations for firms making car finance settlement offers
data.summary:
Research shows consumers want the choice, rather than wait for the legal challenges to conclude.

Almost 9 out of 10 (89%) car finance customers who have complained or are considering doing so want the choice of an offer of compensation now, rather than waiting for the legal challenges to the FCA's compensation scheme to conclude. 86% would be comfortable making the decision, and 61% say they’d accept an offer in line with the scheme. Timing matters for many: 77% say receiving compensation sooner would make a great deal or fair amount of difference to their financial situation.The survey findings are being released today alongside the FCA's expectations for lenders who want to make settlement offers to those owed compensation under its scheme, while legal challenges continue. This comes as Barclays Partner Finance confirms it will make settlement offers to some of its customers owed compensation.The regulator supports lenders making settlement offers, as long as customers are offered no less than they would receive through the scheme.Lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes that they will keep any money received, even if the outcome of the legal challenges means they would have received less. However, they also wouldn’t be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge means they would have been paid more. As consumers can reject an offer and leave their claim to be dealt with under the scheme, these offers can’t be referred to the Financial Ombudsman Service for review.Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA’s general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said:'Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. And it’s clear they want the choice.'Anyone who wants to wait can, and there’s no obligation to agree to the offer. We’ll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means.'To help consumers make informed decisions, the FCA has published a factsheet (PDF) that lenders must share with customers when making settlement offers. Not all lenders are likely to make offers, and those that do may only make them to some customers owed compensation. The FCA will regularly update its website with lenders making settlement offers to help consumers check whether an offer is genuine. Firms are expected to notify the FCA if they plan to make offers.Payouts under the motor finance compensation scheme were due to start this year. The scheme is currently partially suspended, pending the outcome of legal challenges due to be heard between 16 February and 3 March 2027. Under the partial suspension, firms must keep preparing for the scheme and continue progressing complaints as far as possible, but do not need to calculate or pay compensation under the scheme until the legal process concludes.Anyone who is concerned about their car finance deal and has not yet complained should complain directly to their lender. There is information on the FCA website on how to complain for free. There is no need to use a law firm or claims management company, which may charge up to 36% of any compensation, including VAT.Notes to editorsResearch conducted by Kantar, surveying 1,000 motor finance customers online between 25 and 28 June 2026. Findings cited are based on a subset of 590 respondents who said they had made or were considering making a motor finance complaint.Barclays press release.Statement confirming motor finance legal challenge to be heard in February 2027.Statement on the partial suspension of the motor finance scheme and what it means for firms and consumers.

data.title: Demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments
data.summary:
We have seen demands being made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes.

Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries as a way to avoid tax. HMRC has sought to tackle this tax avoidance through what has been termed the loan charge and published guidance for those affected.Questions have been raised about the regulatory status of these loans and whether they were ever intended to be repaid.Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they’re unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.Some consumers are, however being sent legal letters threatening potential court action and asking for immediate repayment of the loan. Repayment is being sought after these disguised remuneration loans were sold by the original provider to a third party.Those seeking payment may ask the FCA to agree to a Validation Order. This is the formal permission needed before the loans could be enforced. We would consider any request carefully and our agreement is by no means guaranteed. If a Validation Order is required and not granted, the debt would remain unenforceable.Anyone who receives a demand for repayment of a disguised remuneration loan, and is unsure whether they are liable for the amount claimed, should consider carefully whether to make any payment. We’d encourage them to look at the HMRC guidance and consider taking legal advice.Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.If you are experiencing any difficulties, whether they are health, money or other difficulties, or if you don't understand what is happening, you should raise this with those contacting you.

data.title: FCA publishes terms of reference for independent review concerning Mr Andriesz
data.summary:
We have published the terms of reference for the review into our handling of interactions with Mr Simon Andriesz, a whistleblower who made protected disclosures to the FCA.

We shared our condolences following Mr Andriesz's tragic death and our thoughts remain with his family and loved ones.The review was commissioned by our non-executive directors. It is being conducted by Lea Paterson CBE, an independent non-executive director of the FCA.When we announced the review, we said it would examine how we interacted with Mr Andriesz. The review will now also look at whether we met our responsibilities under whistleblowing law and followed our own policies and procedures when handling his whistleblowing reports, including his concerns that he had experienced detriment. It will cover the period from at least 2017 to 2026.The review will identify any lessons learned and make recommendations for improvements to our future engagement with external whistleblowers and vulnerable individuals.We previously said we aimed to publish findings in early 2027. Given this broader scope and the need to examine evidence spanning many years, more time is needed to complete the review thoroughly.A progress update will be published in January 2027, with the final report expected in spring 2027.Read the terms of reference (PDF).
